questions.q: According to this lesson, when does lineage documentation start decaying?
options: Almost immediately after it's finished, as the underlying systems keep changing
Only after exactly one year has passed
It never decays once it has been documented correctly
Only if the organization switches lineage tools
questions.explain: Decay is described as the default, not the exception — schema changes, new pipelines, and decommissioned systems all start pulling documentation out of sync right away.

questions.q: Which of these is named as one of the three ordinary reasons lineage documentation decays?
options: A new pipeline is built but never added to the existing graph
The lineage tool vendor changes its company name
A report is viewed by too many users
The organization adopts a new programming language
questions.explain: Schema changes, new pipelines not added to the graph, and decommissioned systems left in as dead nodes are the three ordinary decay reasons this lesson names.

questions.q: What is a 'dead node,' as defined in this lesson?
options: A documented dataset or report that no longer actually exists
A node in the graph with no incoming or outgoing arrows by design
A Critical Data Element that has been deprioritized
A node that has never been assigned an owner
questions.explain: A dead node is a retired system or report still sitting in the documentation, making the graph look more connected and trustworthy than it actually is.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why doesn't automated lineage (Lesson 19) fully eliminate the maintenance burden?
options: Because its blind spot — manual exports, one-off scripts, undocumented steps — still needs a human to revisit on a schedule
Because automated tools cannot be re-run after the first scan
Because automated lineage tools are always more expensive than manual documentation
Because automation only works for relational databases
questions.explain: Automation keeps the scannable, code-based part of the graph current, but the manual, off-pipeline part still needs active human review on a schedule.

questions.q: Which practice does this lesson tie directly to the change impact assessment process from Lesson 15?
options: Reviewing lineage documentation on every change ticket, so it updates as a normal step of the existing process
Re-writing the entire lineage graph from scratch after every change
Deleting all documentation whenever a change is proposed
Removing ownership assignments after each sign-off
questions.explain: Tying a lineage-documentation check into the same change process already used for change impact assessments makes the update happen as a routine step rather than something easily forgotten.
